questions.question: What's driving you to improve your commit messages right now?
questions.why_it_matters: A contributor to open-source projects needs Conventional Commits, signed commits, and PR-friendly footers; a team member needs ticket-linking and review-oriented context; a solo developer may only need a personal log that stays useful months later.

options.label: Contribute to open source
options.implication: Covers Conventional Commits spec, DCO/sign-off, breaking-change footers, and how maintainers read history

options.label: Work on a professional team
options.implication: Adds ticket-ID prefixes, code-review context patterns, release-note generation, and team-linting setup

options.label: Personal projects / solo work
options.implication: Focuses on the 50/72 rule, imperative mood, and a lightweight personal template — no tooling overhead

questions.question: Which describes your current git fluency?
questions.why_it_matters: Someone who has never run `git commit` needs the staging-area mental model first; someone who already writes `fix: typo` but gets asked to reword needs style guidance, not mechanics.

options.label: Never committed — new to git
options.implication: Prepends a 10-minute git basics module: staging area, commit object, `git log --oneline`, amending

options.label: Commit regularly but messages are vague ("fix", "update")
options.implication: Starts directly with the 50/72 rule, imperative mood, and before/after rewrite exercises

options.label: Already use Conventional Commits, want sharper context
options.implication: Skips syntax; dives into scope granularity, breaking-change footers, co-author trails, and review-oriented body paragraphs

questions.default_label: Commit regularly but messages are vague ("fix", "update")

questions.question: What deliverable would you actually use day-to-day?
questions.why_it_matters: A cheat sheet lives in your editor; a COMMITTING.md becomes the team standard; a prepare-commit-msg hook enforces structure automatically; a commitlint config catches mistakes in CI.

options.label: One-page cheat sheet for myself
options.implication: Produces a printable markdown reference: type list, 50/72 ruler, body checklist, example gallery

options.label: Team CONTRIBUTING/COMMITTING.md
options.implication: Writes a project-level guide with required types, scope list, ticket-link regex, and review checklist

options.label: Git hook or CI lint config (prepare-commit-msg / commitlint)
options.implication: Generates a ready-to-install hook or commitlint config that blocks non-conforming messages locally and in PRs

options.label: Interactive practice repo with exercises
options.implication: Creates a tiny git repo with staged changes and prompts — you write messages, get automated feedback on style

questions.question: What does "clear, conventional" mean for you — which level is the finish line?
questions.why_it_matters: Basics stop at subject/body formatting; Conventional Commits adds machine-parsable types and breaking changes; Advanced adds footers for automation, signing, and complex multi-repo workflows.

options.label: Basics — subject line, body, 50/72, imperative mood
options.implication: Covers only human-readable structure; no type prefixes, no tooling

options.label: Conventional Commits spec (feat:/fix:/chore:, scopes, BREAKING CHANGE:)
options.implication: Implements the full spec so changelog tools and semantic-release can consume history

options.label: Advanced — footers (Refs:, Co-authored-by:, Signed-off-by:), GPG signing, fixup/squash workflows
options.implication: Adds commit signing, GitHub/GitLab trailer parsing, and interactive rebase patterns for clean history

questions.default_label: Conventional Commits spec (feat:/fix:/chore:, scopes, BREAKING CHANGE:)

sequence: Writing Clear, Conventional Git Commit Messages
output.why: All concepts build toward a single coherent capability — writing commit messages that communicate intent and context. They are taught together because each depends on the previous: fundamentals → specification → structure → types/scope/breaking changes → style skills → practices → anti-patterns.

exclusions.topic: Git CLI commands for committing (git commit, git commit --amend, git rebase -i)
exclusions.consequence: Learner knows what a good message looks like but not how to create or edit one in practice.
exclusions.when_to_learn: When they first sit down to write a commit, or when they need to fix a message they already made.

exclusions.topic: Commit signing and verification (GPG, SSH, signed commits)
exclusions.consequence: Cannot prove authorship or meet repository policies that require signed commits.
exclusions.when_to_learn: When a project requires signed commits or they work in a security-sensitive environment.

exclusions.topic: Monorepo and multi-project commit conventions (scopes per package, shared tooling)
exclusions.consequence: Messages become ambiguous in large repositories; tooling like changesets or nx cannot parse them reliably.
exclusions.when_to_learn: When working in a monorepo or contributing to a project with per-package versioning.

exclusions.topic: CI/CD integration (automated changelogs, version bumping, release triggers from commit messages)
exclusions.consequence: Cannot leverage commit messages for automation; manual release processes remain.
exclusions.when_to_learn: When setting up or maintaining a release pipeline that consumes conventional commits.

exclusions.topic: Git hooks for message validation (commit-msg, prepare-commit-msg, Husky, commitlint)
exclusions.consequence: No automated guardrails; poor messages enter history and must be caught in review.
exclusions.when_to_learn: When they want to enforce conventions locally or in a team setting.

covered.why: Establishes what a commit is, why messages exist, and what makes them valuable — the foundation for everything else.
Provides the standard format the target capability explicitly asks for; defines the contract all later concepts follow.
The core mechanism — learner must be able to produce each part correctly and know when each is required.

covered.concept: Commit types (feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore)
covered.why: Essential vocabulary for communicating intent; learner must choose the right type fluently.
Adds contextual precision; learner needs to know when and how to apply it, not just that it exists.
High-stakes signal; learner must recognise when it applies and format it correctly.
Style convention that directly affects clarity; requires practice to internalise (not just understand).
Directly satisfies 'communicate context' in the target capability; learner must produce bodies that explain why and what changed.
Common traceability practice; learner needs to know the syntax and when to include references.
Affects message clarity — atomic commits make messages focused and meaningful; bundled changes force vague messages.

covered.concept: Common anti-patterns (vague messages, mixed changes, missing context)
covered.why: Negative examples cement the positive rules; learner recognises what to avoid in their own writing.

modules.title: Writing Clear, Conventional Git Commit Messages
covers: Commit types (feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore)
Common anti-patterns (vague messages, mixed changes, missing context)
modules.why_here: Every concept is a necessary piece of the single target capability: writing a complete, conventional commit message that communicates intent and context. None stands alone as an exercisable skill — types without structure are useless, structure without types is empty, style without practice doesn't stick. They form one teachable unit.
modules.capability: Write a complete conventional commit message — including correct type, optional scope, imperative subject, descriptive body explaining the why and what, breaking-change footer when needed, and issue/PR references — and recognise and avoid the common anti-patterns that undermine clarity.
